meta.title: Cloud Security Academy
meta.subtitle: From the fundamentals to incident response: 12 lessons, 36 questions, 12 value deliverables.
meta.disclaimer: Educational material. Practice in test accounts; do not make changes in production without authorization.

lessons.title: The shared responsibility model
lessons.summary: The provider secures the infrastructure of the cloud; you secure what you put and configure in it. Most incidents happen on your side of the line.
points: The provider (Microsoft Azure; the same goes for AWS or GCP) protects the security "OF the cloud": data centers, hardware, physical network, hypervisor.
You protect the security "IN the cloud": identities and permissions, data, service configuration, virtual network, and the operating systems you manage.
The line moves with the service: in IaaS (a VM) you patch the operating system; in PaaS or SaaS the provider does more, but identities, data and configuration are always yours.
Rule of thumb: if you can change it from your console, securing it is your responsibility.

practice.label: Free path on Microsoft Learn: security, compliance and identity concepts

quiz.q: A company uploads customer data to an Azure Blob Storage container and leaves it with anonymous access by mistake. Whose responsibility is it?
options: Microsoft, because the storage account lives on its infrastructure
The company: configuration and data are its part of the model
quiz.why: Service configuration and data are "security in the cloud": always the customer's, in any type of service.

quiz.q: In which of these services do you have to patch the operating system?
options: A SaaS service such as Microsoft 365
quiz.why: In IaaS you manage the VM's operating system, including its patches. In PaaS/SaaS the provider does it.

quiz.q: Which responsibility do you keep even in a SaaS service?
options: The physical security of the data center
The identities, permissions and the data you store
quiz.why: Identities, access and data are never transferred to the provider: that is why MFA and permissions are your first line of defense.

vbd.deliverable: A one-page responsibility matrix (RACI) for 3 cloud services your team uses.
done_when: 3 real services listed with their type (IaaS, PaaS or SaaS)
For each one: what the provider secures and what your team secures
A named owner for every control that is on your side
Reviewed with your lead or with the service owner
vbd.value: Nobody assumes "the cloud already protects it": every control on your side has an owner.

where.label: Use Microsoft's official model as a reference

resource_notes.shared_es_azure: The same model in Azure: useful if your company uses more than one cloud.

lessons.title: Risk and threat modeling
lessons.summary: Before choosing controls, ask what can go wrong. STRIDE gives you six threat categories to review any design.
points: Risk = likelihood × impact. Not everything is protected the same way: prioritize what would do the most damage.
The CIA triad sums up what we protect: Confidentiality, Integrity and Availability.
STRIDE: Spoofing, Tampering, Repudiation, Information disclosure, Denial of service and Elevation of privilege.
Threat modeling is a team exercise over a diagram: what are we building? what can go wrong? what will we do about it? did we do a good job?

practice.label: Draw the diagram of one of your team's apps and review it with STRIDE

quiz.q: An attacker uses stolen credentials to log in as another user. Which STRIDE category is it?
quiz.why: Spoofing is pretending to be another identity. It is mitigated with strong authentication (MFA).

quiz.q: Which property of the CIA triad is lost if someone modifies database records without permission?
quiz.why: Integrity = data is not altered without authorization.

quiz.q: What is the best way to prioritize threats?
options: Handle the newest ones in the news first
By likelihood × impact on what matters most to the business
In the alphabetical order of STRIDE
quiz.why: Risk = likelihood × impact: focus the effort where the potential damage is greatest.

vbd.deliverable: A STRIDE threat model of a real application or flow of your team.
done_when: Diagram with components, data flows and trust boundaries
At least one threat reviewed for each letter of STRIDE
The 3 highest-risk threats with their proposed control and owner
Stored where the team can find it (wiki, repo)
vbd.value: Controls are chosen by the real risk of the system, not out of habit.

lessons.title: Misconfigurations: the number one cause
lessons.summary: Most cloud leaks do not come from sophisticated attacks but from something misconfigured: public data, excessive permissions, open ports.
points: Typical mistakes: blob containers with anonymous access, network security groups (NSGs) open to the internet, roles with excessive permissions, diagnostic logs turned off.
The pattern repeats in every cloud: a small flaw in an app becomes a massive leak when that app's identity (its managed identity or service principal) can read far more than it needs.
Preventing is cheaper than detecting: disable anonymous blob access on the storage account, use Azure Policy to block insecure configurations and deploy from reviewed templates (Bicep or Terraform).

The Microsoft cloud security benchmark (MCSB) and the CIS Microsoft Azure Foundations Benchmark list the recommended secure configuration; Microsoft Defender for Cloud measures your environment against them.

practice.label: Review the Microsoft cloud security benchmark

quiz.q: A web app has a vulnerability that lets an attacker act with the app's managed identity. What turns that flaw into a massive leak?
options: The identity having more permissions on storage than it needs
A physical failure in the data center
quiz.why: The attacker inherits whatever the identity can do: if it could only read one container, the damage is bounded; if it could read everything, everything is lost.

quiz.q: Which control prevents any container in a storage account from becoming public?
options: Disabling "Allow Blob anonymous access" on the storage account
quiz.why: With anonymous access disabled on the account, no container can be made public even if someone tries by mistake.

quiz.q: An NSG allows RDP (port 3389) from "Any" or "Internet". What does that mean?
options: That only the internal network can get in
That any internet address can try to connect over RDP
quiz.why: "Any" or "Internet" is the whole internet. Restrict it to known IPs or use access without exposed ports: Azure Bastion or Defender for Cloud just-in-time access.

vbd.deliverable: A report of 5 risky configurations found in a test subscription or in your team's.
done_when: Review of public storage, ports open to the internet, MFA and logs
Each finding with its severity (high/medium/low) and the related benchmark control (MCSB or CIS)
At least 1 finding fixed or with an open ticket
Shared with the subscription owner
vbd.value: You close the doors that cause the most leaks before someone finds them.

lessons.title: Identity and least privilege with Entra ID and Azure RBAC
lessons.summary: Identity is the new perimeter: every person and every service should have only the permissions it needs, and not one more.
points: Least privilege: grant only the actions and resources needed for the task, and remove them when they are no longer used.
Prefer managed identities and just-in-time access with PIM over long-lived secrets and standing permissions.
Assign roles to groups and at the smallest possible scope (resource or resource group), not person by person across the subscription.
Measure what is really used with access reviews and sign-in logs, and trim what is left over.

practice.label: Azure RBAC best practices on Microsoft Learn

quiz.q: An application on an Azure virtual machine needs to read a single blob container. What is the right approach?
options: Store the storage account access key on the server
A managed identity with the Storage Blob Data Reader role on that container only
Give it the Contributor role on the whole subscription to avoid problems
quiz.why: Managed identity (no secret to store) + minimum role + specific scope = least privilege.

quiz.q: Why are managed identities and short-lived tokens preferred?
options: There is no secret to store and tokens expire on their own: if they leak, they are useful only briefly
quiz.why: A leaked long-lived key or secret works until someone revokes it; a token expires in minutes or hours.

quiz.q: What helps trim access nobody needs anymore?
options: Access reviews in Microsoft Entra ID Governance
quiz.why: Access reviews ask periodically who still needs a role or a group, and remove whatever is not confirmed.

vbd.deliverable: A permissions review of 5 identities (people or services) with a plan to trim them.
done_when: 5 identities reviewed with their current role assignments
Permissions unused in 90 days identified
Proposed assignments with a specific role and scope (no unnecessary Owner or Contributor)
At least 1 change applied or approved
vbd.value: If a credential leaks, the possible damage is bounded.

lessons.title: MFA, SSO and Global Administrator accounts
lessons.summary: A stolen password should not be enough to get in. Phishing-resistant MFA, single sign-on and Global Administrator accounts kept under lock and key.
points: MFA blocks the vast majority of password-theft attacks; turn it on for everyone, starting with administrators.
Not all MFA is equal: SMS < authenticator app codes < number-matching notification < FIDO2 keys/passkeys (phishing-resistant).
SSO with Microsoft Entra ID centralizes joiners, leavers and MFA: when someone leaves the company, they are disabled in one place; Conditional Access decides when to ask for more proof.
Global Administrator: few accounts, with phishing-resistant MFA and activated through PIM only when needed; plus two emergency access accounts monitored with alerts.

quiz.q: Which type of MFA resists phishing best?
quiz.why: FIDO2 verifies the site's real domain: a fake site cannot reuse the response.

quiz.q: What is the correct use of an emergency access (break-glass) account?
options: Real emergencies only, with phishing-resistant credentials and an alert every time it is used
Shared by the IT team for day-to-day work
quiz.why: It is the last door when normal sign-in fails: it is kept apart, almost never used, and every use is investigated.

quiz.q: What advantage does SSO give when offboarding a person?
options: They are disabled in one place and lose access to all connected accounts and apps
It changes every password in the company
quiz.why: Without SSO you have to delete users in each system, and one gets forgotten.

vbd.deliverable: An MFA inventory of your team with a plan to close the gaps.
done_when: List of privileged accounts and their type of MFA
Global Administrator accounts verified: few, with phishing-resistant MFA and activation through PIM
Accounts without MFA or with SMS identified, with a date for the change
Alert configured (or requested) for when an emergency access account is used
vbd.value: A leaked password is no longer enough to take over your tenant.

lessons.title: Secrets: keys, passwords and tokens
lessons.summary: A secret in the code or in a chat ends up leaking. Store it in a manager, give it minimum access and rotate it.
points: Never in code, repositories, tickets or chats: repositories get cloned and git history does not forget.
Use Azure Key Vault as the secrets manager: encryption, access control with RBAC and auditing. Better still, use managed identities so there is no secret to store.
Rotation: change secrets periodically and immediately if a leak is suspected; better if it is automatic.
Scan repositories (GitHub secret scanning, Gitleaks) to catch keys before they reach production.

practice.label: Run a secrets scanner (e.g. Gitleaks) on one of your team's repositories

quiz.q: You pushed a storage account key to a public repository by mistake and deleted it in the next commit. What do you do?
options: Regenerate the key immediately and review its use in the logs
Make the repository private and that is it
quiz.why: The key is still in the history and bots scan GitHub within minutes: regenerate it and review what was done with it.

quiz.q: What does Azure Key Vault add over a .env file on the server?
options: Encryption, per-identity permissions, an audit trail of who read it, and rotation
quiz.why: Key Vault centralizes and records access; a loose file does not tell you who read it.

quiz.q: What is the best rotation practice?
options: Rotate periodically and immediately on suspicion, ideally automated
Rotate once a year by hand
quiz.why: Automatic rotation shortens the window in which a leaked secret can be used, without relying on someone's memory.

vbd.deliverable: A secrets inventory of an application with its migration to Azure Key Vault.
done_when: Secrets scan run on the repository, with results
Each secret listed with where it lives today and who uses it
At least 1 secret migrated to Key Vault and read from the app with a managed identity
Rotation policy defined (frequency and owner)
vbd.value: Keys stop living in places where anyone can copy them.

lessons.title: Encryption at rest and in transit
lessons.summary: Encrypt the data you store and the data that travels. The hard part is not encrypting: it is managing the keys well.
points: In transit: TLS (HTTPS) on every connection, internal ones too; disable old protocols (TLS 1.0/1.1).
At rest: Azure encrypts storage and managed disks by default; decide where you need customer-managed keys (CMK).
Azure Key Vault (or Managed HSM) holds the keys; envelope encryption uses one data key per object, protected by a key encryption key (KEK).
Whoever controls the key controls the data: limit who can use each key and log its use.

quiz.q: What does encryption in transit protect?
options: Data while it travels over the network
quiz.why: TLS protects the communication from being read or altered along the way.

quiz.q: In envelope encryption, what does the key that lives in Key Vault (the KEK) encrypt?
options: The data key that in turn encrypted the file
quiz.why: The Key Vault key never leaves the service; it encrypts small data keys, which are the ones that encrypt the data.

quiz.q: Why does it matter who can use a Key Vault key?
options: It does not matter if the data is encrypted
Whoever can use the key can decrypt the data
To comply with the language requirement
quiz.why: Encryption moves access control to the key: its permissions are as important as the data's.

vbd.deliverable: An encryption map of a system's sensitive data.
done_when: Stores with sensitive data listed (databases, storage accounts, disks, backups)
Encryption status at rest and in transit for each one
Who can use each key, reviewed
Gaps with a plan and an owner
vbd.value: You know which data would be readable if a disk, backup or connection were exposed.

lessons.title: Network security and Zero Trust
lessons.summary: Segment the network to limit the attacker's movement, and stop trusting something just because it is "inside".
points: Segment: public subnets only for what must receive internet traffic; databases and internal services in private subnets.
Network security groups (NSGs) filter statefully per subnet or per network interface; Azure Firewall inspects centrally. Use minimal rules.
Avoid opening administration ports: use Azure Bastion, just-in-time access or a VPN with MFA, and reach PaaS services through private endpoints.
Zero Trust: always verify identity, device and context on every access; never trust based on network location alone.

quiz.q: Where should a production database live?
options: In a public subnet with a public IP
In a private subnet or behind a private endpoint, reachable only from the app
In any subnet as long as it has a password
quiz.why: A database does not need to receive internet traffic: isolating it drastically reduces its exposure.

quiz.q: What does it mean that an NSG is stateful?
options: That it keeps a copy of the traffic
That the reply to an allowed connection passes automatically, without a rule in the opposite direction
That it only works with IPv6
quiz.why: The NSG remembers each allowed flow: the reply to an allowed inbound connection needs no outbound rule.

quiz.q: What does the Zero Trust principle state?
options: Everything inside the corporate network is trusted
Never trust by default: verify every access with identity and context
Distrust the cloud provider and do not use it
quiz.why: Zero Trust moves trust from "being on the network" to "proving who you are and under what conditions" on every access.

vbd.deliverable: A network diagram of a system with its exposure rules reviewed.
done_when: Diagram with public/private subnets and allowed flows
Rules open to "Any" or "Internet" justified or removed
Administrative access with no ports open to the internet (or a plan to get there)
Reviewed with whoever operates the network
vbd.value: A compromised server can no longer reach everything else.

lessons.title: Containers and Kubernetes
lessons.summary: A container is as secure as its image, its permissions and the cluster it runs on.
points: Images: minimal official base, vulnerability scanning in the pipeline and in Azure Container Registry (Defender for Containers), no secrets inside.
Runtime: do not run as root, read-only file system where possible, no privileged containers.
Kubernetes (AKS): authentication with Microsoft Entra ID, least-privilege RBAC, namespaces, network policies and secrets kept out of the image.
The control plane (API server) never exposed to the internet without strong authentication; in AKS consider a private cluster or authorized IP ranges.

practice.label: Scan one of your team's images (Defender for Containers in Azure Container Registry, or Trivy)

quiz.q: Why is it risky to run a container as privileged?
options: It can take control of the host node if the container is compromised
quiz.why: A privileged container has almost the same powers as the host: an escape compromises the whole node.

quiz.q: Where should the passwords used by an application in Kubernetes go?
options: In variables written in the Dockerfile
In Azure Key Vault or Kubernetes Secrets with restricted access
quiz.why: The image is copied to registries and machines; secrets must be injected at runtime with controlled access.

quiz.q: What does RBAC control in Kubernetes?
options: Which users and service accounts can perform which actions on which resources
quiz.why: RBAC is the IAM of Kubernetes: it applies least privilege inside the cluster too.

vbd.deliverable: A security checklist applied to one of your team's containerized services.
done_when: Image scanned, with critical and high vulnerabilities listed
Verified: it does not run as root or privileged
Secrets kept out of the image
The service's RBAC permissions reviewed
vbd.value: A vulnerability in the app does not turn into control of the cluster.

lessons.title: Logs and monitoring
lessons.summary: Without logs no investigation is possible. Record who did what, protect it from deletion and centralize it.
points: Send the Azure activity log and the Microsoft Entra ID logs (sign-ins and audit) to a Log Analytics workspace with a diagnostic setting.
Protect the logs: a separate workspace or subscription, or immutable storage; an attacker usually tries to delete them first.
Centralize in Microsoft Sentinel (SIEM) to correlate events from several sources and alert.
Define retention according to legal and investigation requirements: the activity log is kept for only 90 days unless you export it.

practice.label: Activity log in Azure Monitor (Microsoft Learn)

quiz.q: What does the Azure activity log answer?
options: Who did what operation, when and from where
quiz.why: It is the basic forensic record of the cloud.

quiz.q: Why store logs in a separate workspace or in immutable storage?
options: So that an attacker with access to the affected subscription cannot delete them
quiz.why: Erasing traces is a typical attacker step; separating the logs or making them immutable prevents it.

quiz.q: What does a SIEM such as Microsoft Sentinel provide?
options: It centralizes, correlates events from several sources and generates alerts
quiz.why: Correlating sources reveals attacks that cannot be seen in a single log.

vbd.deliverable: A log coverage map of your cloud environment.
done_when: Activity log and Entra ID logs exported in every subscription
Log destination protected from deletion (separate workspace, immutable storage)
Retention defined and documented
One useful alert created (e.g. use of an emergency account or a role assignment change)
vbd.value: When an incident happens you can answer what happened instead of guessing.

lessons.title: Threat detection and posture (CSPM)
lessons.summary: Let managed services watch for you: detection of anomalous behavior and continuous review of configuration against standards.
points: Threat detection (Microsoft Defender for Cloud plans and Microsoft Defender XDR): they analyze logs, identities and network to find malicious behavior.
Posture (CSPM: Defender for Cloud and its Secure Score): continuously compares your configuration against the Microsoft cloud security benchmark.
A finding without an owner is useless: define who receives each severity and how fast it is handled.
Start with a few high-quality alerts; too much noise causes the important ones to be ignored.

practice.label: What is Microsoft Defender for Cloud? (Microsoft Learn)

quiz.q: What is the difference between threat detection and CSPM?
options: Detection looks for malicious activity; CSPM checks whether the configuration meets standards
quiz.why: One watches what is happening; the other, how the environment is built.

quiz.q: Microsoft Entra ID Protection reports a sign-in from an anonymous IP address (Tor network) using a user's credentials. What do you do first?
options: Validate with the owner and, if they do not recognize it, revoke their sessions, reset the password and review what was done
Turn off the detection to clear the alert
Wait to see whether it happens again
quiz.why: Contain first (sessions and credentials) and then investigate the scope in the sign-in and activity logs.

quiz.q: Why is it better to start with a few high-quality alerts?
options: Because the tools charge per alert
Because too much noise makes the team ignore the important ones too
Because there are no other types of alert
quiz.why: Alert fatigue is a frequent cause of incidents that were detected but nobody handled.

vbd.deliverable: A posture dashboard with the top 10 gaps and their plan.
done_when: Defender for Cloud (posture and detection) enabled in a subscription (test or real)
Top 10 recommendations prioritized by severity and exposure
An owner and a date for each one
Routing rule: who receives each severity
vbd.value: Gaps are found and closed continuously, not only at the annual audit.

lessons.title: Incident response in the cloud
lessons.summary: When something happens, a rehearsed plan is worth more than the best tool: prepare, detect, contain, eradicate, recover and learn.
points: NIST 800-61 cycle: preparation → detection and analysis → containment, eradication and recovery → post-incident activity (lessons learned).
Revision 3 (2025) integrates response with NIST CSF 2.0: governance, identification and protection are also part of responding well.
In Azure, containing usually means: revoking sessions and credentials, isolating resources (a quarantine NSG) and taking disk snapshots for the investigation.
Rehearse with tabletop exercises and write runbooks for the most likely scenarios.

quiz.q: A virtual machine is confirmed to be compromised. What is best for the investigation?
options: Isolate it (network quarantine) and take a snapshot before making any change
quiz.why: Deleting or restarting destroys evidence; isolating contains the damage and the snapshot preserves the state.

quiz.q: In which phase of the NIST cycle are runbooks written and drills carried out?
quiz.why: Everything you do before the incident (plans, access, tools, rehearsals) is preparation.

quiz.q: What is the lessons-learned phase for?
options: To improve the controls and the plan so the same incident does not happen again
quiz.why: A blameless review turns the incident into concrete improvements.

vbd.deliverable: A response runbook for a likely cloud scenario, tested in a tabletop exercise.
done_when: Scenario chosen (e.g. a leaked key or secret) with detection criteria
Containment, eradication and recovery steps with owners
Contacts and escalation defined
A 30-minute tabletop exercise done with the team, with improvements noted
vbd.value: On the day of the incident the team runs a plan instead of improvising.

glossary.definition: The split of security between the cloud provider (the cloud) and the customer (what they put and configure in it).
Infrastructure as a service: you rent virtual machines, network and disks; you manage the operating system.
Platform as a service: the provider manages the operating system and you manage the application and the data.
Software as a service: you use a finished application; you remain responsible for identities and data.
Confidentiality, integrity and availability: the three properties that security protects.
Threat categories: spoofing, tampering, repudiation, information disclosure, denial of service and elevation of privilege.
The exercise of identifying what can go wrong in a design and which controls mitigate it.
Cloud Security Posture Management: continuous review of cloud configuration against standards.
Secure configuration guide recommended by the Center for Internet Security for a product or cloud.
Server-Side Request Forgery: the attacker makes the server send requests on their behalf, e.g. to the metadata service.
Identity and access management: who can do what on which resources.
Giving only the permissions needed for a task and removing them when they are no longer used.
A set of permissions assigned to an identity at a scope: subscription, resource group or resource.
An identity that Azure creates and rotates for a resource, so it can reach other services without storing secrets.
Multi-factor authentication: something you know plus something you have or are.
Authentication with a cryptographic key bound to the domain, resistant to phishing.
Single sign-on: one central identity to get into many applications.
A Global Administrator account reserved for when normal sign-in fails; it is protected, almost never used and every use raises an alert.
A service that stores, encrypts, audits and rotates passwords, keys and tokens.
Changing a secret periodically or when a leak is suspected.
Protection of data while it travels over the network, usually with TLS.
Protection of data stored on disks, databases or storage.
The Azure service that stores and controls cryptographic keys, secrets and certificates.
Data is encrypted with a data key, which in turn is encrypted with a key encryption key (KEK).
The protocol that encrypts and authenticates connections (the HTTPS padlock).
A private network inside Azure where your resources live.
A subnet with no direct route from the internet, for internal services and databases.
A stateful traffic filter associated with a subnet or a network interface in Azure.
A private network interface inside your VNet to reach a PaaS service without exposing it to the internet.
A model that does not trust based on network location: it verifies identity and context on every access.
Dividing the network into zones to limit an attacker's lateral movement.
A container with permissions almost equal to the host's; compromising it reaches the node.
Role-based access control; in Kubernetes it defines what each user or service account can do.
Automatic review of known vulnerabilities in container images.
The record of operations on a subscription's resources: who did what, when and from where.
A system that centralizes and correlates security events from many sources and generates alerts.
The length of time logs are kept.
The Microsoft service that assesses security posture (CSPM) and detects threats in cloud workloads.
The output of a security tool that points to a possible problem.
Loss of attention caused by too many alerts, which leads to ignoring the important ones.
The process to prepare for, detect, contain, eradicate, recover from and learn from an incident.
Actions to stop the damage of an incident, such as revoking credentials or isolating resources.
Removing the cause of the incident (malware, access, configurations).
A copy of a compromised resource's disk, to investigate it without altering it.
A step-by-step procedure to respond to a specific scenario.
A talked-through simulation of an incident to test the plan and the roles.
A blameless post-incident review that turns the incident into improvements.
